nodes.label: [B]/[C]/[S] Dialect-Tagging Convention
nodes.rationale: The Alexander & Elias-Bursać textbook explains (p.23, lesson 2) that bracket tags mark either (a) a pan-BCS word with a restricted-area alternate, or (b) two competing words with different regional preference. Recurs across every lesson 1-11 as the primary mechanism for encoding national-standard variation directly in vocabulary.
nodes.community_name: BCS Grammar Core: Case, Aspect & Jat Reflex

nodes.label: Clitic Second-Position Placement Rule
nodes.rationale: Short/clitic forms (se, short 'to be' forms, object pronoun clitics, future auxiliary ću/ćeš/će) must occupy the clause's second position regardless of where the main verb falls. A strict multi-slot ordering among co-occurring clitics (li - aux - dat - acc/gen - se - je) is elaborated across Lessons 6, 9, and 10.
nodes.community_name: BCS Grammar Core: Case, Aspect & Jat Reflex

nodes.label: Adjective Comparison: Suffix -ij- and Consonant-Softening
nodes.rationale: Two productive comparative patterns: suffix -ij- (vàžan->vàžniji) or stem-final consonant softening (kràtak->kraći), plus four suppletive comparatives (dobar/bolji, loš/gori, vèlik/veći, mali/manji). Superlative always prefixes naj- to the comparative. Softening set (k->č, g->ž, h->š, t->ć, d->đ...) is shared with passive-participle and verbal-noun formation.
nodes.community_name: BCS Grammar Core: Case, Aspect & Jat Reflex

nodes.label: Dative-Experiencer / Subjectless Sentence Construction
nodes.rationale: States/feelings put the experiencer in the dative with the verb 3sg and the state expressed as an adverb (dosadno mu je 'he's bored'). Generalized in Lesson 10 to accusative-subject 'fear' constructions (strah me je) and genitive-subject quantity constructions (mnogo ih ima).
nodes.community_name: BCS Grammar Core: Case, Aspect & Jat Reflex

nodes.label: Dative/Locative/Instrumental Plural Syncretism
nodes.rationale: Lesson 6 grammar point: although dative, locative, and instrumental are distinct singular cases, all three collapse to one shared plural form per noun (-ama for feminine -a nouns, -ima for everything else). The singular Dative/Locative also fully coincide.
nodes.community_name: BCS Grammar Core: Case, Aspect & Jat Reflex

nodes.label: Ekavian/Ijekavian (Jat Reflex) Split
nodes.rationale: Historic Common Slavic jat reflects as -e- (Ekavian, chiefly Serbia proper) vs. -je-/-ije- (Ijekavian, chiefly Bosnia, Croatia, Montenegro, southwestern Serbia). This is a regional pronunciation axis that cuts across the B/C/S national-standard split rather than mapping onto it 1:1 (explicit in Lesson 9's Cyrillic-exercise note: Ijekavian Serbs exist in Bosnia/SW Serbia/Montenegro).
nodes.community_name: BCS Grammar Core: Case, Aspect & Jat Reflex

nodes.label: BCS Future Tense (hteti/htjeti-based Auxiliary)
nodes.rationale: Compound future = clitic/full auxiliary (from hteti/htjeti 'want') + infinitive or da+present. Croatian keeps infinitive+ću as two words; Serbian fuses them into one word; Bosnian permits both. The clitic auxiliary carries only future meaning, while the full form is ambiguous with 'want.'
nodes.community_name: BCS Grammar Core: Case, Aspect & Jat Reflex

nodes.label: Genitive Case and Its Uses
nodes.rationale: Introduced Lesson 4: masc/neut genitive singular is identical to the animate accusative; feminine takes -e or -i. Governs many prepositions (iz, kod, od, bez, posle/poslije, itd.), the invariant existential nema, and partitive-vs-whole direct-object contrasts (Lesson 5).
nodes.community_name: BCS Grammar Core: Case, Aspect & Jat Reflex

nodes.label: Inclinational se-Construction
nodes.rationale: 3sg verb + se with the experiencer in dative expresses feeling like (or not) doing something (meni se spava 'I feel sleepy'). B/C nè da se vs. Serbian nè da mi se is flagged as a genuine cross-dialect semantic divergence of the same phrase.
nodes.community_name: BCS Grammar Core: Case, Aspect & Jat Reflex

nodes.label: Prepositions of Motion Toward a Person (k/ka vs. do/kod)
nodes.rationale: Croatian uses k(a) + dative for movement toward a person; Bosnian/Serbian instead use genitive-governing do (to a person) and kod (to a person's house) -- a genuine B/C/S grammatical-construction split, not just a lexical one.
nodes.community_name: BCS Grammar Core: Case, Aspect & Jat Reflex
nodes.norm_label: prepositions of motion toward a person (k/ka vs. do/kod)

nodes.label: Passive Participle Formation (-n/-t/-en)
nodes.rationale: Three markers (-n, -t, -en) attach to the infinitive or present stem depending on conjugation type, with -en requiring consonant softening for types 2/3/15 (postaviti->postavljen, videti/vidjeti->viđen). Some verbs vary between two markers.
nodes.community_name: BCS Grammar Core: Case, Aspect & Jat Reflex

nodes.label: Past Tense (biti auxiliary + L-participle)
nodes.rationale: Periphrastic past tense: present tense of biti + an L-participle agreeing with the subject in gender/number. Formation varies by the verb's one of 16 conjugation types (fully tabulated Lesson 10); the auxiliary can drop in certain narrative styles (fairy tales).
nodes.community_name: BCS Grammar Core: Case, Aspect & Jat Reflex

nodes.label: Verbal Aspect (Perfective/Imperfective)
nodes.rationale: Introduced Lesson 2 (kupiti/kupovati), formalized Lesson 6 and Lesson 10: most BCS verbal ideas have paired perfective (single/completed action) and imperfective (repeated/ongoing/general) verbs, formed by prefixation or suffixation, sometimes corresponding to distinct English verbs.
nodes.community_name: BCS Grammar Core: Case, Aspect & Jat Reflex

nodes.label: Reflexive Possessive svoj vs. njegov/njen
nodes.rationale: svoj marks 'one's own' possession referring back to the subject, contrasted with person-specific possessives like njegov ('his'); formally introduced Lesson 5 A3 vocabulary box.
nodes.community_name: BCS Grammar Core: Case, Aspect & Jat Reflex

nodes.label: u-words vs. na-words (Locative Preposition Lexical Class)
nodes.rationale: Individual nouns are lexically fixed as taking either u ('in') or na ('on/at') for locative sense, independent of English usage; a few words shift meaning by which preposition attaches (u selu 'in a village' vs. na selu 'in the countryside').
nodes.community_name: BCS Grammar Core: Case, Aspect & Jat Reflex
nodes.norm_label: u-words vs. na-words (locative preposition lexical class)

nodes.label: 16 BCS Verb Conjugation Types
nodes.rationale: BCS verbs are grouped into 16 types by the infinitive-to-present-stem relationship (type 1 = a-conjugation, types 2-4 = i-conjugation, remainder = e-conjugation). Identical-looking infinitives (e.g. dovesti/dovedem type 13 vs. dovesti/dovezem type 14) can belong to different types, so each verb's infinitive+1sg-present must be memorized as a pair.
nodes.community_name: BCS Grammar Core: Case, Aspect & Jat Reflex

nodes.label: Three-Way 'Take/Carry' Verb Root System (nos-/vod-/voz-)
nodes.rationale: BCS distinguishes carrying an inanimate object or a being who must be carried (nositi), leading a being that moves under its own power on foot (voditi), and moving a being by vehicle (voziti). Their perfective partners exist only prefixed, with distinct roots -nes-/-ved-/-vez-.

nodes.rationale: Source flags Banja Luka/Banjaluka as both spelled as two words and as one, with three attested accusative forms (Banja Luku, Banjaluku, Banju Luku) -- a genuine orthographic-variation note kept distinct from the book's [B]/[C]/[S] register tags.

nodes.rationale: pdftotext's linearization of Lesson 5's two-column A1 vocabulary box paired 'pet' (five) with the gloss 'fifth' and vice-versa; the extraction subagent caught and corrected this using the independent numeral chart on the same page rather than trusting the raw column order.

nodes.label: Aorist and Imperfect: Archaic/Literary Past Tenses
nodes.rationale: Two single-word past tenses, now largely confined to (especially older) literary texts: the aorist relates individual completed actions in sequence, the imperfect describes ongoing background states/actions. Both survive in spoken Serbian/Bosnian mainly in fossilized colloquial idioms (odoh ja, 'I'm out of here'). Lesson 17's poem 'Zemlja' drills all three past tenses (compound past, aorist, imperfect) together for nuanced shading; Lesson 19's Genesis excerpt is tagged aorist-vs-imperfect as a dedicated exercise; both appendices catalogue the forms formally.
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Archaic Tenses & Aspect Pairing
nodes.norm_label: aorist and imperfect: archaic/literary past tenses

nodes.label: Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian Regional Lexical-Variant Tagging
nodes.rationale: The textbook's bracket convention ([B], [C], [S], and combinations) marks genuinely distinct word choices between the three national standards for the same meaning (e.g. trgovina/dućan/radnja 'store'), as opposed to the purely phonological E/J split. Appears in every lesson, both grammar appendices, and all three glossary parts in this chunk; occasionally extends to three-way splits and to onomastics (personal names).
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Archaic Tenses & Aspect Pairing

nodes.label: Ekavian/Ijekavian (E/J) Jat-Reflex Alternation
nodes.rationale: Single most pervasive systematic phonological/orthographic split in the whole BCS corpus: the historical yat vowel surfaces as 'e' (Ekavian, centered on Serbia) vs. 'je'/'ije' (Ijekavian, Bosnia/Croatia/most of Montenegro), affecting nouns, adjectives, verbs, and whole vocabulary-box headers ('RJEČNIK [J] REČNIK [E]') across every lesson 12-20 and both grammar appendices. Distinguished by the source from the separate lexical-choice [B]/[C]/[S] tagging convention.
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Archaic Tenses & Aspect Pairing

nodes.label: Relative Conjunction/Pronoun koji
nodes.rationale: Unlike English 'who/whom/which/that', BCS can never omit koji. Its gender/number agree with its antecedent; its case is fixed independently by its own clause-internal grammatical role (e.g. kojoj is feminine singular but locative when governed by a preposition in its own clause). Taught in Lesson 12, elaborated with worked case examples in Lesson 13, and drilled again (without re-explanation) in Lesson 18's B3 exercises.
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Archaic Tenses & Aspect Pairing

nodes.label: Present and Past Verbal Adverbs (Converbs)
nodes.rationale: Present verbal adverb: unchanging suffix -ći on the imperfective 3rd-plural present stem, marks simultaneous action (vozeći se autobusom čita novine). Past verbal adverb: suffix -vši replacing final -o of a perfective L-participle, marks prior-completed action, used only in written style. A handful of each type (idući, sljedeći, vodeći, mogući, odgovarajući; bivši) have calcified into full adjectives. Reviewed again as the mechanism drilled in Lesson 14's OLUJA/CRNA HRONIKA/MAGLA reading passages and catalogued formally in Appendix 6/9's verb-form inventory.
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Archaic Tenses & Aspect Pairing

nodes.label: Verbal Aspect: Imperfective/Perfective Pairing
nodes.rationale: Nearly every verb in the corpus is glossed with an (I)/(P) aspect marker and frequently paired with its aspectual partner (e.g. dospeti/dospijem P vs. imperfective counterparts). Lesson 15 gives the fullest explicit discussion: imperfective signals ongoing/habitual/general-fact meaning, perfective signals a single completed (or, contextually, repeated-but-bounded) action, and aspect choice organizes narrative structure (perfective advances plot, imperfective sets scene).
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Archaic Tenses & Aspect Pairing

nodes.label: Conditional Mood: Formation and Functions
nodes.rationale: Formed from the L-participle plus an aorist-descended auxiliary (bih, bi, bi, bismo, biste, bi). Functions taught in this lesson: politeness formula (željela bih preferred over blunt želim), toned-down statements/requests, the three-way conditional-sentence typology (ako+indicative / kad+conditional / da+present...conditional), and a purpose-clause use (da bih) with no direct English parallel.
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Archaic Tenses & Aspect Pairing

nodes.label: Reciprocal "Each Other": jedan drugi
nodes.rationale: English 'each other' is expressed either with a reflexive se-verb, or with jedan drugi (two participants) vs. jedni drugi (larger group) — BCS must specify group size where English does not. The second element takes whatever case the verb/preposition governs; gender agreement (Lesson 16) is fixed by the referents' combined gender: masculine if all-male or unspecified, feminine if all-female, neuter if mixed-gender.
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Archaic Tenses & Aspect Pairing

nodes.label: Dative Logical-Subject / Experiencer Constructions
nodes.rationale: A cluster of impersonal verbs/idioms in which the BCS grammatical subject (nominative, triggers agreement) corresponds to the English object, while the affected person sits in an oblique case: nedostajati + Dat ('nedostajao mu je Zagreb' = literally 'Zagreb was missing to him' = 'he missed Zagreb'), poći za rukom + Dat ('it worked out for him'), and stalo [mu je] do + Gen ('it matters to him'). Three separate constructions the source itself cross-references as structurally parallel.
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Archaic Tenses & Aspect Pairing

nodes.label: Indefinite "-ever" Constructions: god / bilo
nodes.rationale: Two competing strategies for forming English '-ever' indefinites: the particle god attached after a question word (kad god 'whenever', gdje/gde god 'wherever'), and bilo prefixed to a question word (bilo šta/bilo što 'whatever', bilo koga 'whomever'). Both recur as drilled review material in Lesson 19's C1 homework sentences.
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Archaic Tenses & Aspect Pairing

nodes.label: Montenegrin as a Distinct Ijekavian BCS Variant
nodes.rationale: The textbook's one explicit acknowledgment of a fourth national standard beyond its own [B]/[C]/[S] system (it advises Montenegrin-focused learners to follow the [J] and [S] forms rather than assigning a dedicated bracket letter). Three concrete markers given: (1) systematic ijekavian character extending into negated-biti forms (nijesam/nijesi vs. standard nisam/nisi) and archaic-elsewhere adjectival endings (starijem vs. starim); (2) tj/dj realized as ć/đ (tjerati->ćerati, djevojka->đevojka, gdje->đe); (3) a handful of characteristic words/pronunciations (sjutra, zboriti). Illustrated via a 1935 Milman Parry field-recorded epic song sung by Stanko Pižurica.
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Archaic Tenses & Aspect Pairing
nodes.norm_label: montenegrin as a distinct ijekavian bcs variant

nodes.label: BCS Case/Declension System (Six Cases + Vocative + Count Form)
nodes.rationale: Nouns/adjectives/pronouns decline for six cases (Nominative, Accusative, Genitive, Dative/Locative syncretic in the singular for most classes, Instrumental) plus a separate Vocative and, for masculine nouns after 2-4, a distinct Count Form. Organized by declension class (masc. animate/inanimate, neuter, feminine -a, feminine consonant-stem), each with mobile-vowel and irregular-stem subtypes. Prepositions govern specific cases and several (na, u, po) switch case by motion-vs-location meaning — the same case-government machinery drilled across Lessons 12-20's grammar points.
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Archaic Tenses & Aspect Pairing
nodes.norm_label: bcs case/declension system (six cases + vocative + count form)

nodes.label: 16-Type BCS Verb Conjugation System
nodes.rationale: The textbook's pedagogical device for predicting a verb's present-tense paradigm from its infinitive: 16 numbered types (plus 2 mixed subtypes and an irregular class outside the system) defined by the infinitive-ending/present-stem relationship, each represented by a model verb pair (infinitive + 1sg present, e.g. igrati/igram). Governed by an accent-shift rule (leftward for Types 1-2, 6-9, 11, 16; rightward for Types 10, 13-15) signaled in print by italicized infinitives. Appendix 9 sorts roughly 500 verbs from Lessons 1-20 into this system; Appendix 6 gives the fuller paradigm tables.
nodes.community_name: Flagship Textbook: Archaic Tenses & Aspect Pairing

nodes.label: Sarajevo/Zagreb Syllable-Switching Slang
nodes.rationale: The single most important content finding in this language's whole corpus: a footnote in Bazdulj's 'Ljubav na španjolski način' (p.354) describes a genuine, historically attested colloquial word game — switching a word's two syllables (zdravo -> vozdra 'hi', kažem -> žemka '(I) say', dođi -> đido 'come!', bježi -> žibje 'run!') — associated with Sarajevo colloquial speech, plus an older 1960s-Zagreb layer (mali -> lima 'kid', braco -> cobra 'bro', Mišo -> Šomi, Franjo -> Njofra), explicitly contrasted with Belgrade's own extensive but non-syllable-switching slang system. Now confirmed independently a second time via a structurally different mechanism: taboo-avoidance substitute-naming practices documented in the Serbian Folk Tales corpus (established/084, established/088) — both are systematic word-formation slang/register mechanisms layered onto standard BCS lexemes, one phonological (syllable-switch) and one semantic (taboo substitution), suggesting BCS-area vernacular register formation productively exploits multiple independent word-formation strategies. This connection is noted here as context only; no cross-chunk edge is created since 084/088 are not part of this chunk's own node set.
